@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission runs a full permission evaluation for every group resource on each user search and count, costing O(groups) policy evaluations per request.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The PR renumbers the exit codes (RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE 4→3, and 4 is reused for FEATURE_DISABLED), but testFeatureNotEnabled and testWrongVersions only check messages, not exit codes. WHY: The exit code is the documented contract for automation scripts, so a wrong or swapped value (for example, feature-disabled reported as recreate) would pass the suite. HOW: Assert `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED, cliResult.exitCode())` in testFeatureNotEnabled and `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE, result.exitCode())` after each incompatible check in testWrongVersions.

The PR makes exit code 4 (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) a documented contract for the feature-disabled case, but this test only checks the error text. It would still pass if the gate exited with 0 or with 3 (RECREATE), which would make automation such as the operator read the result wrongly. Assert `cliResult.exitCode()` equals `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`.

This test only asserts that a message is absent, so it would still pass if `--features=rolling-updates` were not honoured and the command stopped with the feature-disabled error. Add a positive assertion that the metadata command actually ran, such as `assertMessage("Metadata:")` or an exit-code check of 0.

issues.descricao: testFeatureNotEnabled only covers the metadata subcommand, so the feature guard in the check subcommand is untested.

comentarios.texto: testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the `metadata` subcommand and never the `check` subcommand. Removing the feature guard from UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() would therefore not fail any test. It also doesn't assert the exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED=4). Add a case for `check` and assert the exit code on both.

WHAT: testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand disabled path and never the check subcommand. WHY: the feature gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run can be removed or broken without failing any test since no assertion covers its disabled message/exit code. HOW: also launch/assert the check command without --features (e.g. parameterize over metadata and check subcommands or add a second Launch).

testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the metadata subcommand, leaving the identical ROLLING_UPDATES gate in UpdateCompatibilityCheck unverified. If the Check gate were removed, the suite still passes. Parameterize/add a second @Launch for {UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityCheck.NAME} (with required --file or not) asserting the disabled message and FEATURE_DISABLED exit code.

issues.descricao: The disabled-feature test checks only the error message, not that the command exits with FEATURE_DISABLED (4).

comentarios.texto: The new disabled-feature test only verifies the error text, not the failure exit status. If the metadata command still prints this diagnostic but exits with 0 (or another incorrect code) instead of FEATURE_DISABLED (4), this test would still pass. Assert that cliResult.exitCode() equals CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED so the test actually protects the new disabled-feature failure contract.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: getCredential always calls getFederatedCredentialsStream first. For LDAP-federated users this runs LDAPStorageProvider.getCredentials, which queries LDAP and throws IllegalStateException when the LDAP object is not found. WHY: recovery-code login and the RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean page now fail with a 500 (and pay an LDAP round-trip on every call) for federated users whose recovery codes are stored locally, where before only local storage was read. HOW: check local stored credentials first and only fall back to the federated stream, or only consult the federated provider when it supports the recovery-codes type.

WHAT: when user storage accepts the new recovery codes, the local `createCredential` is skipped, and that call is the only place an existing local recovery-codes credential gets deleted. WHY: UserCredentialManager.isValid still runs the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider, so codes the user meant to replace by regenerating still authenticate. HOW: when userStorageCreated is true, remove any existing local recovery-codes credential.

WHAT: the user-storage path serializes the raw plaintext recovery codes (`generatedCodes`) into the UserCredentialModel, while the local path stores only the hashed codes from credentialModel. WHY: any user storage provider receives and may persist plaintext recovery codes, so a leak of the external store exposes working second-factor codes. HOW: pass the hashed credential data (credentialModel.getCredentialData()) to the user storage instead of the raw codes.

WHAT: the credential can now come from user storage, but when all codes are used it is still deleted with `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only acts on the local store. WHY: a federated credential (whose id may be null when built via createFromValues) is never removed from the user storage, so the exhausted credential stays configured. HOW: when the credential has a federation link or came from the federated stream, remove it through the storage provider (e.g. disableCredentialType) instead of removeStoredCredentialById.

The error log hard-codes the credential type as "recovery-codes", but RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE is "recovery-authn-codes". Anyone reading the log or searching for the type will be pointed at a type that does not exist. Use the constant so the message stays correct.

`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but once all codes are used the authenticator still deletes it with `removeStoredCredentialById`. That call only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB, so the federated credential stays in user storage and the user is still treated as configured for recovery codes. Remove it through a path that handles federated credentials too, e.g. `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById` only when the credential is local, and `updateCredential`/`disableCredentialType` against user storage when it is federated.

isValid returns true if the input matches any generated code (anyMatch), but the login page asks for one specific code number (getNextRecoveryAuthnCode). A user can enter any of their codes instead of the requested one and still pass, so this does not behave like the local provider. The check should compare the input only against the code at the expected (next unused) index.

getCredentials builds a new model with createFromValues instead of returning the stored CredentialModel, so the id generated in updateCredential is not passed through. Anything downstream that relies on the credential id gets a different or null id, for example removeStoredCredentialById in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator or account credential listing. Set the id on the rebuilt model from myUser.recoveryCodes.getId().

`RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` now read the federated credential through `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`. They assume a successful `isValid` uses up the accepted code, so the next requested code number moves forward and `allCodesUsed()` can eventually be true. This `isValid` accepts any stored code and never removes it, so every login asks for code #0, codes can be replayed, and regeneration is never triggered. After a successful match, check the input against the requested next code and remove it from the stored JSON list.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

issues.descricao: Creating recovery codes in external storage does not remove a previously stored local recovery-codes credential, and validation falls back to local storage, so the replaced codes still authenticate.

comentarios.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

issues.descricao: Exhausted recovery codes are removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which only covers local storage, so a federated recovery-codes credential is never removed.

comentarios.texto: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key), but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so the value is a datetime. WHY: build_cursor calls this key on the result rows and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError, so every non-empty optimized_pagination request returns a 500. HOW: Convert datetimes to epoch milliseconds, as DateTimePaginator.get_item_key does, or subclass DateTimePaginator.

WHAT: value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, and build_queryset puts it directly into a `datetime <= %s` filter for the '-datetime' key. WHY: Comparing an integer millisecond timestamp to a datetime column either fails in the database or filters the wrong rows, so following any next/prev cursor is broken. HOW: Convert the cursor value back to a UTC datetime, as DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does.

WHAT: When enable_advanced_features is set, a client-supplied negative cursor offset is passed straight to queryset[start_offset:stop]. WHY: Django QuerySets reject negative indexing with ValueError/AssertionError, and paginate() only catches BadPaginationError, so a cursor like `0:-5:0` gives an unhandled 500. HOW: Reject negative offsets by raising BadPaginationError, or clamp them to 0.

WHAT: enable_advanced dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access on every request, and member can be None for non-superuser principals that pass OrganizationAuditPermission without an org membership. WHY: Because the line runs before the use_optimized check, those requests now raise AttributeError and return a 500 even when the default paginator would have been used. HOW: Check use_optimized first and guard against a missing member.

The comment says the Django ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically", but `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The comment states the reverse of what this branch actually does, so it presents a crashing path as safe. Correct the comment, or clamp the offset so the code matches the documented behaviour.

The new comment in BasePaginator.get_result says passing a negative offset through for prev cursors is safe "because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions". Django querysets reject negative slice indices with a ValueError instead of handling them. The comment documents a guarantee that does not exist.

The endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" to OptimizedCursorPaginator, but that paginator's get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the key value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value. Those are numeric-key semantics, not DateTimePaginator's datetime handling. With optimized_pagination=true, any non-empty result raises TypeError when the cursor is built from a datetime. The integer cursor value would also be compared against the datetime column without conversion. Either make OptimizedCursorPaginator handle datetime keys the way DateTimePaginator does, or use DateTimePaginator for this datetime-ordered queryset.

When a client sends a negative cursor offset (for example `0:-5:0`), this code slices `queryset[-5:...]`, and Django QuerySets raise an error on negative indexing, so the request fails with a 500. The comment says the ORM handles this, but it does not, and the `is_prev` branch skips the clamp in the same way. Always clamp the start index with `max(0, offset)` before slicing.

The new clamp applies only to forward cursors, so a prev cursor with a negative offset (for example `0:-1:1`, which Cursor.from_string accepts) still slices the QuerySet with a negative start. Django raises on that, and the request returns a 500. Clamp the offset regardless of `is_prev`.

The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on a datetime object, which raises TypeError whenever results are returned. value_from_cursor also passes the raw integer cursor value into the datetime filter instead of converting it back the way DateTimePaginator does. The key handling needs to match DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-epoch conversion in both directions.

The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by='-datetime', so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` raise a TypeError when the cursor is built. Any non-empty request on the optimized path therefore fails. Convert the datetime to an epoch value the way DateTimePaginator.get_item_key does.

value_from_cursor returns the integer cursor value unchanged, and build_queryset compares it against the `datetime` column. Following pages are then filtered on a wrong or invalid value instead of the timestamp the cursor encodes. Convert the cursor value back into a datetime the same way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does.

When advanced features are on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start, and Django QuerySets reject that with an AssertionError or ValueError. A client-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore causes an unhandled exception and a 500. Clamp the offset to 0, or reject negative offsets.

The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` raise TypeError when `build_cursor` computes keys. As a result, every request with optimized pagination crashes. Convert the datetime to epoch milliseconds the same way DateTimePaginator does, and convert it back in `value_from_cursor`.

For `is_prev` cursors the offset is left unclamped, so a negative offset from a client cursor goes into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` and Django raises on the negative index, returning a 500 from every BasePaginator endpoint. Clamp the offset in both directions.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets straight into Django queryset slicing, which Django does not support, so requests with a negative offset raise an error instead of returning a page.
issues.textoGolden: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

comentarios.texto: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

issues.descricao: The comment added to BasePaginator claims negative offsets are allowed and safely handled by the queryset, but the code clamps non-prev offsets to zero and leaves prev offsets as before, so the comment misdescribes the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

issues.descricao: The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring claims streamlined boundary handling, an optimized query path and backward compatibility that the implementation, a copy of BasePaginator plus a negative-offset branch, does not provide.

comentarios.texto: Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator computes cursor keys with math.floor/ceil on the raw attribute, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so building the cursor raises TypeError for any non-empty result.
issues.textoGolden: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

comentarios.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

issues.descricao: The audit log endpoint always dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, which crashes with AttributeError for authorized token requests that have no member, even on the default pagination path.
issues.textoGolden: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

comentarios.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. Authorized non-member organization-token requests therefore raise AttributeError even when optimized_pagination is absent, instead of returning audit logs through the existing paginator. Guard the optional member and evaluate eligibility only when optimized pagination is requested.

issues.descricao: The comments and enable_advanced variable describe the optimized_pagination path as a performance optimization for administrators, hiding that it enables negative-offset slicing.

comentarios.texto: The comments describe a 'performance optimization' for 'authorized administrators', and the variable is named enable_advanced. In fact it opts into negative-offset slicing, and the optimized_pagination query parameter gates it. The names and comments hide what the flag actually enables. Rename them to say what is enabled, or remove the path.

issues.descricao: A user-controlled optimized_pagination flag lets any member with global access switch to a paginator that accepts unvalidated negative cursor offsets, widening the attack surface and causing server errors.

comentarios.texto: A user-controlled `optimized_pagination` query flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that accepts attacker-supplied negative cursor offsets. This is available to any user with global access, not only to real admins. It widens the attack surface for unvalidated cursor offsets and causes server errors. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is not backed by any check in the paginator. Fix: remove the optimized path, or have the paginator validate and clamp offsets.

issues.descricao: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets only for next cursors; a prev cursor with a negative offset is passed straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with an error (500) on every paginated endpoint.
The new comment in Cursor says negative offsets are allowed to enable efficient reverse pagination, but the constructor only calls int(offset) and provides no such behaviour.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: _is_error_focused_query uses a plain substring check, so a query like '!event.type:error' or 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction' is treated as errors-only. WHY: for allowlisted projects on the discover dataset, count() is rewritten to upsampled_count() for queries that exclude errors or include transactions, and the returned counts are wrong. HOW: parse the query with the event search parser and only return True when there is one positive, non-negated event.type:error filter with no OR branches.

WHAT: count() is rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', which always produces a result column named 'count'. With transformAliasToInputFormat=1, the serializer instead looks for the column 'count()', because resolve_axis_column uses the original query_columns in organization_events.py. WHY: for allowlisted error queries that use transformAliasToInputFormat, the series lookup misses and the endpoint returns empty or zero-filled data instead of the upsampled counts. HOW: make the alias of the rewritten column match whatever resolve_axis_column will look up, for example alias it to the original column name when transform_alias_to_input_format is enabled.

The 'no project IDs provided' check runs while the mocked allowlist is still `[]`, so the function returns False through the empty-allowlist check and never reaches the `if not project_ids` guard. If that guard were removed, `all()` over an empty list would return True and every query with no projects would be upsampled, yet this test would still pass. Set a non-empty allowlist before this check.

`_is_error_focused_query` uses a plain substring check, so the negated query `!event.type:error` also matches. That query means "exclude errors", but upsampling still turns on. On the discover dataset, count() then becomes `upsampled_count()` for a query that selects only non-error events (for example, transactions), so the counts returned are wrong. Parse the query, or at least require that the match is not preceded by `!`, before reporting the query as error-focused.

`final_columns` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count() as count`, so the query result series is now keyed `count` (or an `upsampled_count` alias) rather than `count()`. The response serialization (`get_event_stats_data`, which handles multi-yAxis and top-events grouping) still uses the original `query_columns` to look up each series. As a result, multi-axis or top-events responses can drop the upsampled series or put it under the wrong key. Make the transformed column keep the alias that consumers expect (for example the `count()` result key), or map the results back to the original column names before returning.

`_is_error_focused_query` uses a substring test, so `!event.type:error` (and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`) also count as error-only queries. On the discover dataset this applies the `upsampled_count()` / `sample_weight` transform to non-error events, which breaks the rule that the transform only applies to errors. Match the filter as a whole, non-negated token instead of a substring.

issues.descricao: The upsampling decision is evaluated against the request's dataset instead of the scoped_dataset actually queried, so in the dashboard discover-split path (metrics dataset) error queries run against discover skip upsampling even when all projects are allowlisted.
issues.textoGolden: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

comentarios.texto: The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

issues.descricao: _is_error_focused_query uses a substring match for `event.type:error` on the request query, so negated or mixed (OR transaction) discover queries are treated as error-only and get the sample_weight sum instead of count().

comentarios.texto: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

The substring check treats `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as error-only queries. For allowlisted projects this rewrites count() to an aggregation over sample_weight even when the Discover query includes transactions, violating the error-only restriction and potentially failing against a transaction-backed query. Determine the event-type restriction from the parsed query rather than the presence of a substring.

Substring matching does not establish that the Discover query selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True here, causing count() to be replaced with the sample-weight aggregation for non-error or mixed results in allowlisted projects. This contradicts the error-only guard and can produce incorrect counts. Parse the query and establish an error-only restriction (including negation and Boolean structure), or conservatively skip transformation when that restriction cannot be proven.

issues.descricao: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being applied to transaction queries, because the transaction has no sample_weight and upsampled_count() equals count() for it.

comentarios.texto: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events would still pass if upsampling were wrongly applied to transaction queries. The transaction event has no sample_weight, and upsampled_count uses ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so the result is still 1 and 0. Give the transaction a non-default sample rate or weight so an upsampled count would differ from a plain count, or assert that the transform was not applied.

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot falsify over-application of upsampling: the stored transaction has no sample_weight so upsampled_count() (sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) returns 1, same as count(). Give the transaction a sample_weight/client_sample_rate that would diverge (e.g. count 10 if upsampled vs 1 if not), or assert via mock that transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling was not called / yAxes were not rewritten.

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being wrongly applied to transaction queries. The stored transaction event has no error_sampling context, so sample_weight is null, and upsampled_count = toInt64(sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) evaluates to 1 for it — identical to count(). If _should_apply_sample_weight_transform/_is_error_focused_query were broken so that a discover query with event.type:transaction gets upsampled, the assertion count==1 (and 0 in the empty bucket) would still pass. Add an event with a known non-1 sample_weight (or assert the emitted query uses count() and not upsampled_count) so the test actually fails when the transaction exclusion is bypassed.

issues.descricao: The test factory helper's docstring promises a valid client sample rate but it copies any truthy float-convertible value (negative, >1, strings), unlike production validation.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling uses `if client_sample_rate: float(...)` with no type/range check, unlike production _derive_client_error_sampling_rate which requires isinstance(int,float) and 0<rate<=1. WHY: string '0.1', bool True, or out-of-range 5.0 get stored as sample_rate in fixtures while production drops them, making upsampling tests diverge from prod. HOW: mirror production validation before assigning sample_rate.

The new docstring says the client sample rate must be 'present and valid', but the implementation only checks truthiness and float conversion. Negative rates, rates greater than 1, and float-convertible non-finite values are all accepted and written to sample_rate. This falsely tells test authors that this helper enforces sample-rate validity. Either document that it merely copies truthy float-convertible values, or validate the supported sample-rate range and finiteness before setting the field.

issues.descricao: With upsampling active, top-events queries pick and order the top N groups by raw count() (selected_columns/orderby are not transformed) while the plotted series use upsampled_count(), so ranking can disagree with the displayed weighted counts.

comentarios.texto: Only timeseries_columns are upsampled while selected_columns and orderby used to select the Top N remain based on raw count(). discover.top_events_timeseries first queries those unchanged selected columns to choose groups, so a group with fewer retained events but a higher weighted count is omitted in favor of a lower-volume group. Apply the weighted-count transformation consistently to Top N selection and its ordering as well as the displayed timeseries.

issues.descricao: _are_all_projects_error_upsampled and its caller take an organization argument that is never read.

comentarios.texto: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` takes an `organization` argument — also threaded in from the public `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — but never reads it: the body uses only `project_ids` and the global option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. The declared parameter is dead. Either the allowlist check is meant to be organization-scoped (the body must actually consult `organization`) or the parameter should be removed from both functions; as written the signature advertises an organization-scoped decision the implementation never makes.

issues.descricao: Claims only bare count() is rewritten, so aliased count, eps(), epm(), count_unique() etc. stay un-upsampled.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites exact bare `count()` and passes everything else through unchanged. WHY: yAxes like `count() as foo`, `eps()`, `epm()`, `count_unique()`, `count_if()` keep raw counts while should_upsample is true, returning under-counted timeseries. HOW: parse/normalize the function (strip alias, match function name with args) and rewrite all count-equivalent aggs or explicitly fall back to no-upsampling.

issues.descricao: Rewriting count() to `upsampled_count() as count` breaks responses for transformAliasToInputFormat=1: the result column is translated to the rewritten field string while the serializer still reads `count()`.

comentarios.texto: Replacing count() with `upsampled_count() as count` breaks requests using transformAliasToInputFormat=1. QueryBuilder.process_results translates the count alias to the replacement field string, but the endpoint serializer still resolves the original axis as `count()`, so it cannot read the weighted count from the returned rows. Preserve the original public field name in the result mapping when rewriting the internal aggregation.

issues.descricao: upsampled_count truncates the weighted sum with toInt64 instead of rounding, under-counting the estimate by up to one per bucket.

comentarios.texto: `upsampled_count` wraps the sum in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero: `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` of e.g. 1.5 or 3.33 yields 1 or 3 instead of the nearest integer, systematically under-counting the upsampled estimate (worst when weights are just below an integer). Use a rounding aggregation (e.g. `toInt64(round(sum(...)))`) so the reconstructed count reflects the intended estimate rather than a floored value.

issues.descricao: The 'no project IDs' test case runs with an empty allowlist mock, so it passes via the empty-allowlist branch and does not verify the empty project_ids guard.

comentarios.texto: The 'no project IDs provided' case does not exercise the `if not project_ids: return False` guard. mock_options.get.return_value was set to [] just above (line 48), so removing the project_ids guard still returns False via the `if not allowlist` branch, and this assertion passes either way. Re-mock options.get to return a non-empty allowlist (e.g. self.project_ids) before calling with project_ids=[], so the empty-project guard is actually falsifiable.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Every strategy built by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker reuses the single factory-level self.queue_pool, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown() on that shared pool. WHY: After the first partition rebalance, the next strategy submits into shut-down queues. queue.put raises ShutDown, the except in submit() marks the offset complete, and messages are committed without ever being processed. HOW: Create a new FixedQueuePool per create_with_partitions call, or stop shutting down the shared pool in close() and only shut it down in factory.shutdown().

WHAT: _commit_loop calls the arroyo Commit callback from a background daemon thread instead of from the strategy's submit/poll on the main thread. WHY: arroyo's commit changes StreamProcessor state and commits offsets on the KafkaConsumer, which is not thread-safe, while the main thread is polling the same consumer at the same time. This can cause races, lost commits, or commits landing during a rebalance. HOW: Have the background thread (or poll()) compute committable offsets, then call self.commit_function inside poll() on the main thread.

WHAT: Work queues are created as unbounded queue.Queue(), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so arroyo gets no backpressure. WHY: When processing falls behind (the slow-item case this PR targets), the consumer keeps pulling messages and buffering full Message objects in memory without limit, which can exhaust memory and cause a huge redelivery after a crash. HOW: Give each queue a maxsize and, in submit, use put_nowait and raise MessageRejected on queue.Full so arroyo retries the message.

WHAT: get_committable_offsets stops advancing at the first offset in range(start, max+1) that was never added to all_offsets. WHY: Kafka offsets can be non-contiguous (transaction control markers, compacted topics), so a single offset that is never delivered stops commits for that partition forever while all_offsets keeps growing. HOW: Walk the sorted list of seen offsets above last_committed and stop only at the first one that is still outstanding, instead of requiring every integer to be present.

WHAT: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), so each worker exits its while loop after its current item instead of draining the queue. WHY: Items still in the queues are dropped at shutdown, which defeats the graceful drain that immediate=False is meant to provide and forces reprocessing on restart. HOW: Do not set worker.shutdown; let workers drain until get() raises queue.ShutDown.

The docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in a `finally` block (line 149). That marks the offset complete even when `result_processor` raised, so the commit loop commits it anyway. Callers who trust this guarantee will assume failed messages get redelivered, but they are dropped after being logged.

The docstring promises "natural backpressure when queues fill up", but every work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185). As a result, `put` never blocks and the queues can never fill. A reader would wrongly expect memory to stay bounded when workers fall behind.

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes it to every strategy that create_with_partitions builds, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shut that shared pool down whenever partitions are revoked. After a rebalance, the new strategy submits to queues that are already shut down and whose workers have exited. submit() catches the resulting queue.ShutDown and marks the offset complete, so the message is dropped but its offset is still committed. The pool's lifetime belongs to the factory (factory.shutdown() already shuts it down), so the strategy should only stop its own commit thread.

The docstring says processing errors must not block offset commits, but the test asserts that nothing was committed (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). It only waits ~0.2s after processing, while _commit_loop runs about once a second, so it passes because the commit hasn't happened yet and would also pass if a failed item blocked commits forever. Wait for the commit loop and assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

test_preserves_order_within_group submits 5 messages for sub1 but only checks `len(self.processed_results) == 5`. It would still pass if items in the same group were processed out of order. Give each message a unique marker, such as the offset, and assert the processed sequence matches the submit order.

The only assertion is `factory.queue_pool is None`, and ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown sets that unconditionally. The test would pass if queued items were dropped or worker threads kept running. Keep a reference to the pool before shutdown and assert its workers are no longer alive and its queues are empty.

test_concurrent_processing_different_groups only checks that 4 results were processed. It would pass if every group were serialized onto one worker. Check which worker thread handled each group, or block one group and confirm the other group still completes.

The queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every strategy that create_with_partitions builds. close() and terminate() still call queue_pool.shutdown(), so after a rebalance the new strategy submits into shut-down queues. queue.put raises ShutDown, the except block in submit() marks the offset complete, and the message is committed without being processed. Leave pool shutdown to the factory's shutdown(), and only stop the commit thread here.

The loop requires every integer offset between last_committed+1 and max to appear in all_offsets. Kafka partitions can legitimately skip offsets (transaction markers, compaction), so one missing offset stops commits for that partition forever. Messages arrive in order, so the committable offset should be the largest seen offset below min(outstanding), or max(all_offsets) when nothing is outstanding.

Each worker emits remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth using only its own queue's qsize() and only the identifier tag. The gauge ends up showing whichever queue reported last, not a meaningful depth. Add a worker_id tag so each queue gets its own series.

The FixedQueuePool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every strategy that `create_with_partitions` returns, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` shut it down. After the first partition rebalance, the new strategy submits to dead queues: `put` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `submit()` swallows it and marks the offset complete, so offsets are committed for messages that were never processed. Leave pool shutdown to `factory.shutdown()`, which owns the pool, and only stop the commit thread in the strategy.

`_commit_loop` calls the arroyo `commit` callable from its own daemon thread, but that callable stages and commits offsets on the KafkaConsumer, which the StreamProcessor thread drives at the same time. This races with the consumer's own poll/commit/revocation, and the KafkaConsumer is not safe for concurrent use; it can also commit offsets for partitions that were just revoked. Compute the committable offsets in the commit thread if you like, but call `commit_function` from `poll()`/`submit()` on the processor thread.

issues.descricao: Claims OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets requires every integer offset to exist, so Kafka offset gaps permanently block commits for the partition and per-partition state is never cleared on rebalance.

comentarios.texto: Offsets are only tracked for messages that were submitted, and there is no partition revoke handling. Contiguity is checked with `range(start, max_offset+1)`, so any offset gap (compacted topics, transactional markers, or offsets filtered out upstream) permanently blocks commits for that partition. The `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` state is never cleared on rebalance, so stale state survives partition reassignment. Treat gaps as committable once all lower tracked offsets are complete, and clear per-partition state when partitions are revoked.

The commit scan assumes consecutive Kafka offsets and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. A permanent offset gap (compacted or transactional records) then blocks commits for that partition forever. Track the submitted offsets in sorted order and commit up to the highest offset below the lowest outstanding one, rather than requiring every integer in between to be present.

Determine the commit boundary from received offsets rather than requiring every integer in this range to exist. Kafka offsets need not be consecutive: if 100, 102 and 103 are delivered and completed, this scan stops at the nonexistent 101 even though there is no unfinished record. Conversely, after committing 100 and removing it, the next scan starts at 102 and commits past the gap, contradicting the added gap tests. Iterate received offsets in sorted order and stop at the first outstanding record; add a test covering legitimate skipped Kafka offsets across multiple commit cycles.

issues.descricao: OrderedQueueWorker marks a work item's offset complete in a finally block even when processing raised, so failed messages are committed and dropped, contradicting the documented guarantee of committing only after successful processing.

comentarios.texto: The worker marks the offset complete in the `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises, so a message whose handling failed is reported as committable and its offset is committed (it will never be retried). This contradicts the strategy's own guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts the partition is not committed after a failure. Only call `complete_offset` on the success path (or track failed offsets separately) so failures are not silently skipped.

The worker marks the offset complete in `finally` even when `result_processor` raised an exception, so a failed item's offset is reported as committable and gets committed by the commit loop. This contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the contract asserted in test_results_consumer.py (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, which expects the failed partition NOT to be committed): the failed message is committed past and never retried. Track success separately and only call `complete_offset` when processing succeeded (or make the failure explicit so the offset is withheld/retried).

The failed item's offset is completed unconditionally in the `finally` block, so `complete_offset` runs even when `result_processor` raised. This breaks the class's documented guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing', line 254): the commit loop then advances past a message that was never successfully processed, silently dropping it (and, per the PR's own test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, a commit is produced where none is expected). Only call `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` on the success path (i.e. after `result_processor` returns normally), or explicitly decide and document the at-most-once semantics; do not complete on the exception path.

issues.descricao: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's docstring says errors must not block commits for other messages, but the test asserts that nothing was committed, so it does not verify the behaviour it describes.
issues.textoGolden: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

comentarios.texto: The commit assertion contradicts the test's own docstring and cannot fail for the reason it claims. The docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the body asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it passes only when nothing is committed. In queue_consumer.py ordered worker's `finally` calls `complete_offset` even after result_processor raises (lines 148-149), so offset 100 should be committable and offset 101 should advance the commit; if the whole commit path were removed (commits blocked entirely) the test would still pass. Assert the positive behaviour instead: e.g. that the failing message's offset was still completed so commits progressed (expect `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, matching the follow-on offset of the successfully processed message).

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling claims errors don't block commits but asserts len(committed)==0 / not in, and waits only for total==0+sleep(0.2) while commit loop is 1.0s. It passes if commits are correctly made (checked before loop fires) and if commits are never made. Wait for commit condition and assert contiguous commit includes both offsets despite the exception.

issues.descricao: The error-handling test asserts no commit happened after only a 0.2s sleep while the commit loop runs every second, so it passes without ever observing whether a failed offset gets committed.

comentarios.texto: The error-handling test can pass even when failed messages are committed. It waits for two processor calls, sleeps only 0.2 seconds, and asserts that no commit has happened, whereas _commit_loop waits 1 second. OrderedQueueWorker currently completes the failed offset in finally, so the unsafe commit can occur after this assertion. Synchronize with an actual commit-loop iteration before asserting that it cannot advance past the failed offset.

issues.descricao: FixedQueuePool uses unbounded queues and the strategy never applies backpressure, so when workers fall behind the consumer keeps polling and queued work items grow memory without limit, contrary to the documented backpressure guarantee.

comentarios.texto: Each worker queue is created unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) although the class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' and the strategy claims to guarantee backpressure. With no bound and no MessageRejected raised from submit(), a slow group continues to accumulate items in its queue while the consumer keeps polling, so memory grows without limit under a sustained backlog — the opposite of the intended protection. Fix: give the queues a maxsize and raise/return MessageRejected (or otherwise propagate backpressure to the caller) when a queue is full.

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues this strategy drives are unbounded: `FixedQueuePool` creates each one as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185), and `submit()` puts items unconditionally. Nothing ever blocks, so no backpressure exists. Either bound the queues (pass a `maxsize` and handle `queue.Full` / block in `submit`) or correct the docstring so it does not advertise a guarantee the code does not provide.

The pool creates unbounded queues, while strategy submit always accepts messages and poll never applies backpressure. When a queue's worker is slow or ingestion exceeds processing capacity, queued WorkItems retain both decoded results and original Kafka messages without any limit, causing growing memory consumption and eventual consumer OOM. Bound queued/in-flight work and raise Arroyo MessageRejected when capacity is reached, ensuring that rejection is not swallowed by the generic submit exception handler.

issues.descricao: Graceful shutdown sets each worker's shutdown flag before draining, so workers stop with items still queued, and close() stops the commit thread first, so finished work is not committed and gets replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True while OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on while not self.shutdown, so workers exit without draining queued WorkItems even though queues are shut down with immediate=False. WHY: Graceful shutdown silently drops queued items and leaves their offsets in outstanding forever, causing reprocessing/duplicates and failing the claimed graceful-shutdown guarantee. HOW: Remove the shutdown-flag short-circuit and let workers drain until queue.ShutDown, e.g. loop unconditionally and break only on ShutDown.

close() stops the commit thread and shuts down workers before draining accepted work, and join() only repeats close() instead of waiting for processing and making a final commit. Pool shutdown sets worker.shutdown before workers can drain their queues, so assignment revocation abandons queued results and completed in-flight work is not finally committed, causing replay and allowing unfinished old work to overlap a new owner. Make close() stop acceptance without blocking, then have join() drain accepted work within its timeout and commit completed offsets before releasing workers.

Do not set worker.shutdown before draining the queues during graceful shutdown. If a worker is processing A while B is queued, shutdown sets the flag; after A finishes, the worker exits at `while not self.shutdown` without ever retrieving B. Calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not override that loop condition. Drain accepted work before stopping workers, and keep committing available until that drain completes; currently close stops the commit thread before the workers as well, so even work finished during shutdown is not finally committed.

issues.descricao: The strategy's close() shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool, so after a partition rebalance the next strategy reuses a dead pool; submissions fail and the error handler marks their offsets complete, committing messages that were never processed.

comentarios.texto: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is a singleton owned by the factory (created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and never recreated). Arroyo calls strategy.close() then join() on every assignment revocation/rebalance, and the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for the next assignment; the new strategy then reuses the already-shut-down queue_pool. Because q.shutdown(immediate=False) makes subsequent put() raise queue.ShutDown, submit()'s except branch (lines 317-325) swallows it and marks the offset complete, so after any rebalance every message is committed as processed without ever being handled — silent data loss. Fix: either let the factory own the pool lifecycle (don't shut it down from the strategy's close) and create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions, or reset/recreate factory.queue_pool when the strategy is closed.

WHAT: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate shuts down the factory-owned shared FixedQueuePool. WHY: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one queue_pool and hands it to every strategy from create_with_partitions, so Arroyo rebalance (close old strategy, create new one reusing factory.queue_pool) reuses a dead pool with joined workers and shut-down queues, stalling all further processing. HOW: Make pool lifecycle owned only by the factory: strategy close should only stop its commit thread, not call queue_pool.shutdown().

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), terminate() and join() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy it creates. After a rebalance, Arroyo closes the old strategy and then calls create_with_partitions again, which reuses the dead pool. Messages then fail to enqueue, and the submit() exception handler marks them complete, so their offsets get committed without the messages being processed. The strategy should only stop its own commit thread. The pool should be shut down only by factory.shutdown(), or the pool should be created per strategy.

issues.descricao: The strategy invokes Arroyo's commit callback from a background thread rather than from submit/poll on the consumer thread, so commits can race with polling and partition revocation on a non-thread-safe consumer.

comentarios.texto: `commit_function` is called from the background commit thread, but arroyo's commit callback is expected to be called from the main consumer thread, and the Kafka consumer is not thread-safe. Committing from another thread risks races with polling and with rebalances.

issues.descricao: The WorkItem docstring says the original message is kept for offset tracking, but offset tracking only uses partition and offset and the message field is never used.

comentarios.texto: The `WorkItem` docstring says it "includes the original message for offset tracking", but the `message` field is never used for offset tracking — `OffsetTracker` and the commit loop only ever read `partition`/`offset`, and `submit()` even re-derives the offset from `message.value` rather than from the stored `message`. Update the docstring to describe what the field is actually for (or remove the unused field) so it does not misdescribe the dataclass contract.

`WorkItem.message` is declared with the comment 'includes the original message for offset tracking' and is populated in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, but nothing ever reads it — offset tracking uses the separate `partition`/`offset` fields. The declared purpose does not match any actual use, so the field (and the extra reference to each Kafka message it keeps alive) is dead; either use it for offset tracking or remove it.

issues.descricao: The tests named for concurrent processing across groups only check that all items were processed and all groups seen, so a fully serial implementation would pass and concurrency is never verified.

comentarios.texto: Test named/docstringed "Test that different groups are processed concurrently" never verifies concurrency. The body only asserts all 6 items ran and that three distinct group numbers were seen — a single worker draining one queue, or a fully serial FixedQueuePool, would satisfy both assertions. Either measure actual overlap (e.g. have result_processor block on a barrier/event until all three groups have entered, and fail on timeout) or drop the concurrency claim from the name/docstring.

test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions claims to verify that different subscriptions are processed concurrently, but the only assertion is `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`, which a strictly serial implementation also satisfies. Add a real concurrency signal (e.g. a barrier in the mocked processor that requires both calls to be in flight simultaneously before either returns), otherwise this test cannot detect loss of parallelism.

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims concurrent processing but only asserts 6 items processed and 3 groups seen. A serial/single-queue implementation would still pass. Verify overlap (blocking processor + timing/thread IDs) or remove concurrency claim.

issues.descricao: The strategy ordering test submits identical messages and only checks the count processed, so it cannot detect out-of-order processing within a group.

comentarios.texto: The strategy ordering test submits five identical decoded results for sub1 and only asserts their count. Processing them in reverse order would still pass. Give each message a distinguishable sequence value and assert the exact processed sequence, so this tests ordering through SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy rather than only delivery.

issues.descricao: The graceful-shutdown test only asserts that the factory cleared its queue_pool reference, which shutdown always does, so it does not verify that pending work is drained or workers stop.

comentarios.texto: This does not verify graceful shutdown: factory.shutdown unconditionally clears queue_pool after calling pool.shutdown, so the assertion passes even if pending messages are abandoned or worker threads remain alive. Retain the pool reference and assert that all submitted work completed and its workers stopped; the current worker shutdown flag can stop workers without draining their queues.

issues.descricao: The polling bound max_wait = 50 is repeated as a magic number across the thread-queue-parallel tests instead of a named constant.
issues.textoGolden: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

issues.descricao: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets starts scanning at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset); after mark_committed prunes offsets, a gap is skipped on the next cycle, so offsets are committed past a missing offset, contrary to the 'highest contiguous offset' guarantee.
The test's wait loop stops at the first recorded commit but asserts the committed offset is exactly 105, so a commit fired mid-processing can record a lower offset and make the test flaky.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The script now runs ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE on segment keys that consumers on the previous version created with SADD as plain sets, and those keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). WHY: During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after it, Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these keys, so the EVALSHA fails and p.execute() in process_spans raises, crashing the consumer batch. HOW: Use a new key prefix for the sorted-set buffers (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so old and new data never collide, or check the key with TYPE and migrate or skip legacy sets.

WHAT: ZUNIONSTORE is called without AGGREGATE, so it defaults to SUM and adds the scores of a payload that appears in both sets. WHY: A duplicate span (e.g. a Kafka redelivery) ends up with a score of about twice its end timestamp, so ZPOPMIN never evicts it and the eviction no longer follows end time. HOW: Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so a duplicate member keeps its real timestamp.

WHAT: The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data and the limit is now hardcoded as 1000 in add-buffer.lua, so the SpansBuffer `max_segment_spans` parameter (default 1001) is never read. WHY: Any caller or config that sets max_segment_spans is silently ignored, and the effective limit (1000) also differs from the documented default. HOW: Pass self.max_segment_spans to the script as an ARGV value and use it instead of the literal 1000.

WHAT: The redirect-resolution loop bound was cut from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment explaining the limit was removed. WHY: Segment trees whose redirect chains are deeper than ~1000 now stop resolving early and get split into separate segments instead of being joined. HOW: Keep the previous 10000 bound unless the lower depth is an intended limit.

This PR removed the only read of `self.max_segment_spans`, but the constructor still accepts and documents it with a default of 1001. The real cap is now the `1000` hard-coded in add-buffer.lua, and that limit drops the oldest spans instead of skipping the segment. Either pass the configured value into the Lua script, or remove or rename the parameter so its name no longer promises a limit it doesn't enforce.

This PR removed the only Python code that read SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans and hardcoded 1000 in the Lua script instead, so the constructor parameter (default 1001, buffer.py:150/158) is still accepted but has no effect. Callers who set it will get a cap of 1000 regardless, and the default no longer matches the real limit. Pass max_segment_spans to the script as an argument and use it here.

The Lua script now runs `zcard`/`zunionstore`, and flush now runs `zscan`, on `span-buf:s:*` keys that the old code wrote as plain sets (`sadd`). Any set still in Redis at deploy time makes these commands fail with WRONGTYPE. That aborts add-buffer for the whole batch and makes flush fail on those segments until the keys expire. Rename the key prefix (for example to `span-buf:z:`) so old and new data never share keys, or migrate/ignore keys of the old type.

The flush loop no longer checks `self.max_segment_spans`, and the Lua script trims segments to a hardcoded 1000. So the configured `max_segment_spans` value is now ignored. Pass the limit into the Lua script as an argument instead of hardcoding 1000.

Older consumers wrote span-buf:s:* keys with SADD, and those keys can still exist (or keep being written) while the new code rolls out. ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE and ZSCAN on a plain-set key fail with WRONGTYPE, which aborts the add-buffer script and the flush, so whole batches fail until the old keys expire. One fix is to version the key prefix (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so the old and new data layouts can't land on the same key.

The PR removes the Python check against `self.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and adds a hard-coded cap of 1000 in Lua, so the configured limit is never applied anywhere. Any caller that sets a different max_segment_spans silently gets 1000 instead. Pass max_segment_spans into the script as an argument and use it in place of the literal 1000.

issues.descricao: ZUNIONSTORE merges sorted sets with the default SUM aggregate, so a span payload present in both keys gets a doubled end-timestamp score and is wrongly kept by the oldest-first eviction.

comentarios.texto: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

ZUNIONSTORE uses its default SUM aggregation, so replayed payloads present in both the temporary parent_key and the resolved set_key receive the sum of their end timestamps. Replaying a child whose parent already redirects to an ancestor therefore makes that old span score roughly twice its actual timestamp, protecting it from eviction over genuinely newer spans. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN for identical timestamp scores) on both union operations to preserve timestamp scores when members overlap.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both the destination and source has its timestamp doubled rather than preserved. This can happen when a previously merged span is replayed into its original subtree key. The duplicated span then sorts after genuinely newer spans and survives ZPOPMIN eviction incorrectly. Specify AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, since identical payloads should have identical timestamps) on both union calls so merging remains idempotent and scores remain end timestamps.

issues.descricao: Segment keys change from Redis sets to sorted sets under the same key names, so keys left by the previous release make ZADD, ZCARD and ZSCAN fail with WRONGTYPE during rollout, crashing span processing and flushing.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Changed SET ops (scard/sunionstore) to ZSET ops (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no migration breaks in-flight segments. WHY: Old keys of type SET still live up to TTL; ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZADD on the opposite type raises WRONGTYPE and fails inserts/flushes during rollout.

The segment keys were migrated from Redis SETs to SORTED SETs (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN), but nothing handles the keys written by the currently deployed release. During a rolling deploy, an existing `span-buf:s:{...}:{id}` key is still a SET, so this `p.zadd(...)` (and the flusher's `p.zscan(...)`, and the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`) raises WRONGTYPE 'Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value'. That exception is unhandled: it aborts the whole pipeline/Lua invocation and crashes the consumer batch. Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. During deployment, inserting into an existing buffered segment fails with WRONGTYPE, and the new ZSCAN reader likewise fails on pending old-format segments instead of flushing them. Introduce a coordinated migration/drain or a versioned namespace with compatible handling of pending old-format buffers.

issues.descricao: Claims zpopmin eviction can drop the root span while the has-root flag stays set, flushing a segment without its root.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zpopmin eviction by lowest end_timestamp has no protection for the segment/root span. WHY: Root with smallest or tied timestamp (tests use identical timestamps, ties break lexicographically) is evicted while hrs flag stays 1, flushing a root-marked segment missing its root.

issues.descricao: max_segment_spans is still a constructor parameter but is no longer enforced; the segment cap is now hardcoded to 1000 in the Lua script, so the configured value is ignored.

comentarios.texto: This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

buffer.py declares the segment span limit as the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150) and this hunk removed the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` size guard from the flush path, while the other changed file (add-buffer.lua line 62) now enforces a hardcoded cap of 1000 spans. The two changed files disagree on what the segment span limit is: the Lua cap (1000) is not the declared `max_segment_spans`, and the buffer no longer applies the declared limit at all. If `max_segment_spans` is configured below 1000 (or below the Lua cap), oversized segments that this code used to skip will now be flushed. Reconcile the constant: either keep/restore the buffer-side guard against `self.max_segment_spans`, or make the Lua cap derive from the same limit instead of hardcoding 1000.

The segment size cap is hardcoded as 1000 here, but SpansBuffer still declares max_segment_spans = 1001 in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py, and this PR deleted the flush-time guard that used that constant. The declared limit and the actually-enforced limit now disagree (and the Python constant is no longer honored anywhere). Make the Lua cap and the Python constant agree — either pass max_segment_spans in as an ARGV instead of the literal 1000, or update the declared constant to 1000 — so the buffer's enforced bound matches the value it declares.

issues.descricao: Tests give every span the same end timestamp and never exceed 1000 spans, so the new score ordering and oldest-first eviction are not tested.

comentarios.texto: All spans in the fixture use identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the ZSET score-dependent behavior (ordering by end time, zunionstore score merge, and Lua zpopmin keeping newest 1000) is neutralised — tests pass even if scores are wrong or eviction keeps the wrong end. Use distinct timestamps and add a >1000-span trimming test asserting oldest evicted.
The missing test for the new trim path (zset ordering/trim by end_timestamp_precise, the >1000-span zpopmin path) is a coverage gap. Add a test that verifies the new trim behavior.

issues.descricao: The span redirect-walk limit was cut from 10000 to 1000 iterations, so trees deeper than 1000 may not resolve to the correct segment root.
